☆ Homological Barriers to Stable Learning of First-Order Nash Equilibria NeurIPS
Ashkan Soleymani, Gabriele Farina, Patrick Jaillet, Georgios Piliouras
We identify a homological barrier to stable learning of local Nash equilibria, also known as first-order Nash equilibria (FONE), in constrained non-concave differentiable games. We consider continuous deterministic learning dynamics that fix every FONE point and aim to attract all initial conditions to the full FONE set. We show that this convergence guarantee is impossible when the target set has nontrivial positive-degree cohomology, such as that arising from a loop, and the state space is compact and contractible. We exhibit this barrier in a simple non-concave quadratic zero-sum game on a box whose exact FONE set consists of a diagonal six-edge loop and an isolated point. Consequently, no such dynamics can make the full FONE set a stable global attractor. We further show that degree two is the minimal polynomial degree at which this barrier can arise and extend the construction to obtain nontrivial homology in arbitrarily high degrees. Finally, we establish that the barrier persists for sufficiently small approximate-FONE targets under small perturbations, yielding an open, positive-volume family of quadratic zero-sum games with the same homological barrier.

☆ The Complexity of Computing a Competitive Equilibrium in Fisher Markets with Chores
Christian Kroer, Ruta Mehta, Tianlong Nan
We study the complexity of computing competitive equilibria in Fisher markets with divisible chores and positive rational disutility coefficients and earning requirements. For linear disutilities, we prove that exact equilibrium computation is CLS-complete. In particular, the problem remains CLS-hard even when the earning requirements are binary in $1$ and $2^k$, where $k$ is an integer. We prove hardness by encoding the first-order conditions of a box-constrained quadratic program in equilibrium prices and earning flows, using a compact minimum-cost flow construction. For convex constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) disutilities, exact equilibrium prices may be irrational. We formulate the problem of finite-precision equilibrium price computation, in which we seek rational prices with a certified market clearing error at most a given rational tolerance encoded in binary. We prove that this problem is CLS-complete for every fixed rational exponent $ρ>1$. To prove this hardness, we encode a quartic polynomial through the fourth-order expansion of the CES price potential function corresponding to the Eisenberg-Gale (EG) dual program, and show that every sufficiently accurate approximate equilibrium of the constructed market lies near uniform prices. Additionally, we also identify a tractable special case of chores Fisher markets. In particular, we provide a strongly polynomial algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in linear markets whose disutility matrix has rank at most two and earning requirements are arbitrary positive rationals. For $n$ agents and $m$ chores, the algorithm uses $O(nm(n+m))$ rational arithmetic operations and comparisons, with polynomial intermediate encoding length.
♻ ☆ Competition Versus Complexity in Multiple-Selection Prophet Inequalities
Eugenio Cruz-Ossa, Sebastian Perez-Salazar, Victor Verdugo
Competition complexity formalizes a compelling intuition: rather than refining the mechanism, how much additional competition is sufficient for a simple mechanism to compete with an optimal one? We begin the study of this question in multi-unit pricing for welfare maximization using prophet inequalities. An online decision-maker observes $m \geq k$ nonnegative values drawn independently from a known distribution, may select up to $k$ of them, and aims to maximize the expected sum of selected values. The benchmark is a prophet who observes a sequence of length $n \geq k$ and selects the $k$ largest values. We focus on the widely adopted class of single-threshold algorithms and fully characterize their $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity. Notably, our results reveal a sharp competition-induced phase transition: in the absence of competition, single-threshold algorithms are fundamentally limited to a $1-1/\sqrt{2kπ}$ fraction of the prophet value, whereas even a $1\%$ multiplicative increase beyond $n$ observations suffices to achieve a $1-\exp(-Θ(k))$ fraction. Another notable result happens when $k=1$: we show that the $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity is exactly $\ln(1/\varepsilon)$, fully resolving an open question by Brustle et al. [Math. Oper. Res. 2024]. Our analysis is based on infinite-dimensional linear programming and duality arguments.
♻ ☆ Large-Market Discipline in Combinatorial Double Auctions: No Recombination, Bundle Selection, and Complementarities
Konstantinos E. Zachariadis, Yongxin Yang
Licences can forbid assembling bundles from several sellers or splitting them among buyers, a restriction we call No Recombination. We study its welfare cost in a double auction as the number of traders on each side of the market grows. We ask whether that cost vanishes as a share of welfare, as the gain from misreporting does with a single good. With two goods and Gaussian shocks, consider the prices that would prevail under free recombination. As the market grows, the loss as a share of optimal welfare vanishes if and only if expected demand for the two-good bundle equals expected supply of whole bundles at those prices. Otherwise the loss persists. In our market, sellers can never gain by misreporting. With two goods, buyers who commit to bidding their values plus fixed margins misreport in symmetric equilibria by amounts that vanish as the market grows. Under these conditions, in large markets No Recombination outweighs strategic bidding as a source of loss.

♻ ☆ Complexity of Strong Popularity in Hedonic Games
Matan Gilboa
In a hedonic game, agents are partitioned into coalitions and have preferences over the coalitions they may join. A partition is called strongly popular if it strictly beats every other partition in a majority vote among the agents. We study the complexity of determining the existence of strongly popular partitions in two fundamental classes of hedonic games: additively separable and fractional hedonic games (ASHGs and FHGs), where agents' utilities are determined, respectively, by the sum and average of their valuations for the members of their coalitions. We prove that this problem is PCW-complete for ASHGs and for FHGs even with non-negative valuations, where PCW is a subclass of $Σ^P_2$ associated with unambiguous problems (which have at most one witness), recently introduced by Gilboa et al. (2025). These are the first natural complete problems for PCW, in the sense that their formulations do not involve arbitrary Boolean circuits. Our results resolve open problems posed by Brandt and Bullinger (JAIR 2022) and Bullinger and Gilboa (IJCAI 2025). The two reductions employ substantially different techniques, reflecting both the distinct utility models and the stringent non-negativity constraint in FHGs. Furthermore, in contrast with FHGs, we show that in ASHGs restricting valuations to be non-negative makes the problem polynomial-time solvable.

☆ Understanding Spike Encoding across IoT Sensing Modalities: An Empirical Study
Yuxuan Hou, Di Yu, Linshan Jiang, Jin Zhang
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient sensing on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. The input encoder shapes that opportunity by changing the cues available for recognition and the work required to process them. We study these choices across wireless, inertial, surface electromyographic, and tactile sensing. For wireless activity recognition, interleaving reduces estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers, latency from the prepared input window to returned scores, and energy on the graphics processing unit and system-on-chip (GPU/SoC) rail, compared with repeating the full window on Jetson AGX Orin. With the same input size at each SNN time step, repeating a compact input can yield higher mean development accuracy than interleaving. The inertial experiments show that higher accuracy can come at higher device cost. Direct input can also be faster and more accurate than an event encoder while using less energy on the measured rail, even when its estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers is higher. Level crossings improve grasp recognition on a later day for previously observed users. In tactile slip detection, level crossings shift the balance between missed slips and false alarms, and checkpoint selection can reverse which input offers higher slip recall. We use these findings to outline how edge sensing systems can profile encoders against the signal structure, the errors that matter to the task, and the cost of the full inference pipeline.

☆ Neural Activity Synchronization-Based Fast Local Learnable Spiking Neural Network Architecture
Pranith Dutta, Sk Wasim Rajjak, Siddhanta Ray, Santlal Prajapati, Manobendra Nath Mondal
Implementing intelligent learning systems on low- power edge devices is challenging due to the high compu- tational complexity, training latency, and energy demands of traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), biologically plausible and spike-driven, come as an alternative. However, SNN training commonly relies on backpropagation through time (BPTT), which is computationally expensive, inherently global, and unsuitable for battery-driven devices. This work proposes a novel local learning framework for multi-layered SNNs inspired by Neural Activity Synchronization (NAS). Each layer updates its own weights using locally com- puted gradients. No gradient backpropagation is needed. This significantly reduces computational complexity, training latency, and energy consumption. The proposed SNN model is trained and evaluated on the MNIST dataset, achieving a classification accuracy of 97.78%. The model is also analyzed with Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, demonstrating robust performance across different noise levels.
♻ ☆ Boule or Baguette? A Study on Task Topology, Length Generalization, and the Benefit of Reasoning Traces NeurIPS 2026
William L. Tong, Ege Cakar, Cengiz Pehlevan
Recent years have witnessed meteoric progress in reasoning models: neural networks that generate intermediate reasoning traces (RTs) before producing a final output. Despite the rapid advancement, our understanding of how RTs support reasoning, and where this paradigm fails, remain incomplete. To promote greater clarity, we introduce PITA: a novel large-scale dataset of over 23 million statements in propositional logic and their corresponding proofs. As a benchmark for robust reasoning, we focus on length generalization: if a model is trained to determine truth or falsity on statements with proofs up to fixed length, how well does it generalize to statements requiring longer proofs? We propose notions of (1) task depth and (2) task breadth, which measure respectively (1) the number of proof steps required to solve a proposition and (2) the number of unique propositions within a task family. We vary these quantities across subsets of PITA, and find that RT models generalize well on relatively broad and shallow subsets, while deteriorating on relatively narrow and deep subsets compared to non-RT baselines. As a controlled point of comparison, we study a separate, tractable transitive inference task that exhibits qualitatively similar behavior. Our accompanying theory explains the scalings observed in this simpler setting, suggesting one mechanism by which breadth can favor RT models while depth can expose long-context weaknesses. Our findings suggest salient benefits and limitations of proof-like reasoning traces in controlled length-generalization settings.

♻ ☆ From Search to Signal: Search-Value Credit for Evolutionary Automatic Heuristic Design
Yilun Yuan, Tianyu Zhou, Zhenzhou Tang
Large language models generate candidate programs for automatic heuristic design, while evolutionary search evaluates and selects them to guide further generation. Online post-training uses rewards from candidate evaluations to adapt the generator. Retained programs can also guide later generation as parents. This motivates rewards that reflect their reuse opportunities beyond immediate fitness. We propose Search-value credit (SVC), which constructs response-level rewards from actual admission to the retained set and a short-term parent-exposure proxy. Admission determines reward eligibility; the proxy weights eligible responses by reuse opportunities under existing parent-selection rules. Rewards are computed after candidate evaluation, without evaluating descendants. SVC retains the search and learning procedures of the Co-Evolution of Algorithms and Language Model (CALM) framework. Across four combinatorial optimization tasks with the same base model and response budget, SVC achieves the best mean final search performance on three tasks among six conditions. Under identical prompts and parents on traveling salesman and capacitated vehicle routing tasks, SVC-trained generators yield a higher mean proportion of responses whose programs outperform the best prompting parent than those trained with CALM's native reward. These findings support reward construction using search retention and selection information.

☆ The forces at hand: social learning is permissive, not instructive, for the evolution of phenotypic plasticity
Nam H. Le
Evolution can favour a trait for two reasons: an instructive cause makes selection favour the trait; a permissive one lets it persist once selection no longer removes it. The distinction matters most for phenotypic plasticity and its replacement by inherited behaviour, genetic assimilation, the Baldwin effect. Social learning is credited with favouring plasticity on evidence that cannot tell the two apart: how much plasticity remains at the end of a simulation. Here we show, analytically and computationally, which role it plays in a minimal model of learning and evolution. Writing expected fitness as a function of plasticity, we find that environmental change is the only source of benefit from plasticity, and the social channel enters only its cost. Simulation confirms this: in a static environment selection against plasticity never reverses sign at any channel strength; when the environment changes, it reverses at a threshold the channel lowers, and without the channel the population collapses before reaching it. Social learning is permissive, not instructive: it supplies the means to be plastic, never the reason. For the debate over whether plasticity leads evolution, this is one case settled by measurement: environmental change directs, socially inherited information permits, and neither suffices alone.

♻ ☆ On the Adversarial Robustness of Spiking Neural Networks Trained by Local Learning
Jiaqi Lin, Abhronil Sengupta
Recent research has shown the vulnerability of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) under adversarial examples that are nearly indistinguishable from clean data in the context of frame-based and event-based information. The majority of these studies are constrained in generating adversarial examples using Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), a gradient-based method which lacks biological plausibility. In contrast, local learning methods, which relax many of BPTT's constraints, remain under-explored in the context of adversarial attacks. With the increasing real-world deployment of local learning methods in SNNs, it is critical to investigate whether these approaches introduce adversarial vulnerabilities that could compromise reliability. To address this problem, we examine adversarial robustness in SNNs through the framework of four types of training algorithms. We provide an in-depth analysis showing that direct gradient-based attacks are ineffective for locally trained models. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a hybrid adversarial attack paradigm that leverages the transferability of adversarial instances. The proposed hybrid approach demonstrates superior performance, outperforming existing adversarial attack methods. Furthermore, the generalizability of the method is assessed under multi-step adversarial attacks, adversarial attacks in black-box scenarios, and within the non-spiking domain.
♻ ☆ On the Depth of Monotone ReLU Neural Networks and ICNNs NeurIPS 2026
Egor Bakaev, Florestan Brunck, Christoph Hertrich, Daniel Reichman, Amir Yehudayoff
We study two models of $\mathsf{ReLU}$ neural networks: monotone networks ($\mathsf{ReLU}^+$) and input convex neural networks ($\mathsf{ICNN}$). Our focus is on expressivity, mostly in terms of depth, and our motivation is to gain a better understanding of the depth required to exactly represent functions using neural networks with ReLU activations, a subject that has received a lot of attention lately. We prove several lower bounds on the depth required to represent functions by monotone ReLU networks and $\mathsf{ICNN}$. For the maximum function $\mathsf{MAX}_n$ computing the maximum of $n$ real numbers, we show that $\mathsf{ReLU}^+$ networks cannot compute $\mathsf{MAX}_n$, or even approximate it. We prove a sharp lower bound of $n-1$ on the $\mathsf{ICNN}$ depth complexity of $\mathsf{MAX}_n$. We also prove depth separations between $\mathsf{ReLU}$ networks and $\mathsf{ICNN}$s; for every $k$, there is a depth-$2$ $\mathsf{ReLU}$ network of size $O(k^2)$ that cannot be simulated by a depth-$k$ $\mathsf{ICNN}$. The proofs are based on deep connections between neural networks and polyhedral geometry, and also use isoperimetric properties of triangulations.

♻ ☆ DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning NeurIPS 2026
Yuxiang Zeng, Kun Xie, Yang Wang, Jigang Wen, Xiaocan Li, Guangxing Zhang, Gaogang Xie, Jiannong Cao
Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where edge directions determine computational roles and execution dependencies. Existing graph Transformer predictors incorporate topological and directional information in different ways, but primarily focus on specific mechanisms rather than coordinated encoder-wide modeling of these semantics. We introduce encoder-wide directional consistency, a design principle that coordinates the modeling of directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature updates. To implement this principle, we propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer that integrates direction- and topology-aware node initialization, magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative RNN-, CNN-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and magnetic spectral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.

Subhadip Mitra
Note on v2 (Nov 2026): attack success now requires a response judged non-refusing and harmful (v1 counted every non-refusal), so all rates are lower; v1's figures are reported as the non-refusal rate, and with 3 seeds no significance claims are made. Safety alignment in LLMs need not improve monotonically across model generations. Studying four generations of Google's Gemma family (7B-31B) with quality-diversity evolution (MAP-Elites) as an automated red-teaming probe, we find that Gemma 3 (12B) has the highest attack success rate (ASR; response judged non-refusing and harmful): 33.7% +/- 1.3% (mean +/- std, 3 seeds), against 19.0% +/- 10.6% for Gemma 2 and 12.3% +/- 4.2% for Gemma 4. Every Gemma 3 seed exceeds every Gemma 2 and Gemma 4 seed, which we report as directional evidence. Harmful successes rarely transfer between generations (1.4-7.9% ASR when archives are replayed on other generations), lowest on Gemma 4 (1.4-2.8%). Cybercrime is the most exploited category in Gemma 1-3 (47-83%) but falls to 2% in Gemma 4, while misinformation rises from 17% (Gemma 2) to 80% (Gemma 3) and is still 53% in Gemma 4. A second-judge audit (Llama-3.1-70B) confirms 74% of the 8B judge's harmful labels. The non-refusal rate shows the same ordering at 2-3x higher levels and overstates harmful transfer by 6-16x. ♻ ☆ Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
Shivang Rawat, Mirko Morello, Flaviano Morone, David J. Heeger
Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We compensate for this delay by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective, and we develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated temporal band-pass filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs). Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the performance of RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN with built-in attentional modulation and recurrent normalization) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, the prospective variants of these models match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF achieves 83.36% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. We also introduce selective RQFs (sRQFs), which make each filter's input gain and, optionally, its bandwidth and tuning frequency input-dependent while retaining the parallel scan. With the input gain alone, the same six-layer model achieves 86.31% on Path-X; with all three input-dependent, a four-layer prospective sRQF solves Selective Copying (99.83%).

☆ Bridging Spiking and Continuous Dynamics in Spiking Neural Networks: A Muscle-Inspired Model
Maryam Soltani, Philip N. Garner
Transforming the spike trains produced by spiking neural networks (SNNs) into continuous signals through biologically inspired mechanisms remains an open challenge in generative and regression tasks. In biological systems, a similar transformation occurs when muscles integrate neural spikes to produce smooth, coordinated movements. Inspired by this mechanism, we introduce a muscle-response model, a biologically motivated dynamical layer that converts spike trains into continuous representations. Our approach uses second-order dynamics to model the temporal integration of spiking activity. We investigate how the number of spiking neurons and temporal resolution affect the quality of the generated signals in a text-to-speech task, showing that increasing representational capacity has a greater impact than increasing temporal resolution under the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, an analysis of the learned dynamics reveals that, without explicit constraints on the response type, most neurons converge toward non-oscillatory behavior. These results demonstrate the potential of biologically inspired dynamical decoders for bridging spiking neural computation and continuous signal generation.
☆ OMCDE: Opposition-based Multi-Stage Matrix-Based Competitive Differential Evolution CEC
Mohammad Sarhangzadeh, Shahryar Rahnamayan, Doruk Oner
Differential Evolution has proven to be an effective algorithm for continuous global optimization, but it's modern high-performing variants often introduce additional complexity and computational cost. We propose OMCDE, a matrix-based competitive Differential Evolution algorithm that aims to improve optimization performance while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed approach integrates competition-driven search dynamics, adaptive behavior between optimization stages, and opposition-based initialization within a parallelizable framework. These findings indicate that OMCDE is a promising alternative for solving complex numerical optimization problems.

☆ Two-Layer Evolutionary Scheduling for Machine Learning Jobs in Multi-Cluster Environments
Jingyuan Xu, Changwu Huang, Lemeng Pan, Ke Tang, Xin Yao
The rapid growth of large-scale machine learning (ML) workloads has led to unprecedented demands on GPU cluster scheduling systems. However, existing heuristic schedulers struggle to handle the complexity and dynamics of multi-cluster GPU environments, often leading to load imbalance, long queuing delays, and poor alignment to business objectives. This paper formulates the ML scheduling problem in multi-cluster GPU environments as online multi-objective optimization that minimizes the average and maximum weighted queuing times while maximizing GPU time utilization. To solve this optimization problem, we propose EVO-GP, a two-layer evolutionary online scheduling method that decouples global job-to-cluster allocation from intra-cluster GPU resource allocation. At the job-to-cluster allocation layer, an evolutionary algorithm assigns arriving jobs to feasible clusters to promote load balance across clusters. At the resource allocation layer, a priority function automatically learned offline via genetic programming is used to rank jobs and guide GPU allocation within each cluster. Extensive experiments on both real-world data and simulated workloads demonstrate that the proposed EVO-GP method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining superior adaptability and scalability.

CEC 2017 applies bias, shift and rotation simultaneously, obscuring their individual effects on algorithm behavior. We introduce a parameterized implementation controlling them independently while preserving the original functions and transformation data. DSC and eDSC show statistically significant configuration differences at every dimension, but rankings vary across functions, precluding a consistent ordering. Most individual effect-size confidence intervals include zero. Among those excluding zero, comparisons favor MPA more often at dimension 10 and hMPA at dimensions 50 and 100. Shift generally worsens objective-value outcomes. Isolated rotation causes no systematic deterioration; isolated bias barely changes final-solution distributions. Combined shift and rotation differ most consistently from the control. Convergence plots show function- and dimension-dependent separation, plateaus and late improvement. Pietro Barbiero, Giovanni De Felice, Mateo Espinosa Zarlenga, Francesco Giannini, Filippo Bonchi, Mateja Jamnik, Giuseppe Marra, Ruggero Noris
As Artificial Intelligence models grow in complexity, interpretability has become an indispensable tool for understanding, debugging, and controlling their computations. However, interpretability lacks general theories to deductively design interpretable methods. This gap between theories and methods results in a fragmented literature and inconsistent evaluation protocols. To fill this gap, we introduce the Standard Interpretable Model (SIM), a general theory that enables the deductive design of interpretable methods from first principles. Specifically, the SIM summarises, in a set of premises, what interpretability is for a target entity. ☆ SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

☆ Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
Christof Fehrman, Jacob J. Morra, Eva A. Naumann
Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.

Benjamin Jacob Bodner
The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; https://github.com/BjBodner/amm-optimizer).

Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.

Biasing parent selection toward the signals with the strongest measured association to survival nevertheless does not improve search: moderate bias matches uniform sampling, and strong bias reduces QD-score.

Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

Together, the Darwin Family demonstrates that diagnostic-guided evolutionary merging is a practical and reproducible alternative to costly post-training pipelines for reasoning-centric language models.

♻ ☆ Diffusion models for eye-gaze trajectory generation using position and velocity representations
Laxman Basnet, Alexander Szorkovszky, Pedro G. Lind, Anis Yazidi, Shailendra Bhandari
Eye-tracking data are expensive to collect, requiring specialized hardware and controlled laboratory conditions, and difficult to share due to privacy regulations, which together limit the quantity and diversity of gaze data available for research. We investigate unconditional gaze generation using diffusion models in position and component-wise velocity representations. The models are trained and evaluated on eight-second visual-search trajectories from 28 participants, using a split of 23 training participants and five held-out validation participants, with three training seeds. Evaluation includes kinematic distributions, trajectory geometry, event statistics, and a temporal Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty as a learned comparator. Across eight position-derived features, mean Jensen-Shannon divergence is $0.016 \pm 0.004$ for the position model and $0.037 \pm 0.002$ for the velocity model, with standard deviations calculated across training seeds. These scores do not establish that representation choice caused the difference. A separate comparison using the same evaluation method shows that the ordering of the models varies across training seeds. The position model also produces smaller feature discrepancies than a kinematic Markov baseline. Differences in saccade counts between real and generated data depend strongly on the velocity threshold used to detect events. The results provide quantitative reference measurements for unconditional gaze generation on this visual-search task and show how evaluation choices affect conclusions about generated gaze.

♻ ☆ Correlations Are Ruining Your Gradient Descent
Joshua Offergeld, Nasir Ahmad
Natural gradient descent, and the preconditioned optimizers which have followed from it, correct gradient descent by estimating curvature and applying its inverse to the gradient. For any single layer of a deep neural network, this correction can be shown to approximately separate into two factors: one which accounts for correlations in the gradient signal, and one which accounts for correlations in the data arriving at that layer. Herein we show that this second factor can be expressed as a change of basis rather than of curvature and, considered thus, it can be removed from the optimizer entirely and placed within the network itself. Specifically, we show that, once forward weights are corrected, right-sided natural gradient descent can be implemented in a form which has three exactly equivalent forms: a gradient preconditioner, a decorrelating linear transform in the forward pass, or a set of recurrent dynamics in which all updates are Hebbian and rely only upon locally available signals. The (recurrent) decorrelation method we discover aligns closely with proposed methods for inhibitory learning and homeostatic plasticity in the brain. Notably, our transform requires no matrix inverse, no matrix decomposition, and no information beyond that which is available at an individual synapse. It can therefore be applied in distributed and physically constrained systems, including neuromorphic hardware and nervous systems, where existing preconditioners cannot. We demonstrate its effectiveness empirically in convolutional and residual network models while significantly improving a range of approximate biologically plausible methods for credit assignment.

♻ ☆ Subspace Node Pruning
Joshua Offergeld, John Chidiac, Marcel van Gerven, Nasir Ahmad
Node pruning is the art of removing computational units such as neurons, filters, attention heads, or even entire layers to significantly reduce inference time while retaining network performance. In this work, we show that a broad family of importance measures, from activation-based to Fisher-based, share a common quadratic form. Through a lower-triangular change of basis, this form yields a pruning subspace in which entire nodes can be removed while the impact of the lost units is simultaneously recovered via linear least squares. Furthermore, the importance measures within our subspace are decoupled and additive through an orthogonalization of the layer activations, allowing multi-node pruning within layers without interference between importance scores. Our method, Subspace Node Pruning (SNP), outperforms the compared baselines on VGG-16 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet. On OPT-125M and LLaMA-2 7B, SNP matches the state-of-the-art LLM Surgeon at a 40-shot schedule and outperforms it whenever fewer shots are used, all without any retraining after pruning.

♻ ☆ Hardware-Aware Model Inversion in Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
Pablo Sorrentino, Fernando M. Quintana, Erika Covi, Fatih Turkmen
Hardware-accelerated spiking neural networks (SNNs) implemented on memristive crossbar arrays offer significant gains in energy efficiency, while device variability and analog noise are sometimes assumed to hinder information extraction. However, whether these hardware effects improve, preserve, or degrade privacy after deployment remains largely unexplored. Therefore, we ask whether model-inversion leakage characterized on an SNN remains representative after the same model is mapped to a non-ideal memristive substrate, and how hardware non-idealities and reliability faults affecting synapses, neuron thresholds, and spike processing reshape that leakage. To study this problem, we introduce Spiking Domain Model Inversion (SDMI), an inversion method that combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) with surrogate gradients to optimize inputs through stochastic analog behavior and non-differentiable spiking dynamics. We use SDMI consistently across the SNN model, its memristive SNN, and the same memristive SNN under additional hardware perturbations. Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.

♻ ☆ Cultural Evolution Drives the Emergence of Conventions in Neural Emergent Communication
Maxime Toquebiau, Jérôme Botoko Ekila, Paul Van Eecke, Katrien Beuls
Recent studies of language evolution with neural agents often use models where agents can either speak or listen, where there are only two agents in the population, or where agents can share internal representations. These choices prevent the study of how language emerges through cultural evolution, i.e. through the cumulative adaptation of individual behaviours to fit the communicative needs of the community. We tackle this issue with a new model that trains populations of bi-directional neural agents in a fully distributed fashion to solve a referential game. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple image datasets and show that it is able to scale to large populations. We also show that more conventional languages are easier to learn, providing a direct advantage for cultural transmission. Overall, this work provides a novel approach to neural emergent communication that opens up new directions for evolutionary linguistics.
♻ ☆ FiTS: Interpretable Spiking Neurons via Frequency Selectivity and Temporal Shaping NeurIPS 2026
Jongmin Choi, Joon Son Chung
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are a promising framework for event-driven temporal processing. Prior work has improved temporal modeling through richer neuron dynamics and network-level mechanisms such as recurrence and delays, but it remains unclear how individual spiking neurons should specialize within a network. In this work, we introduce FiTS, a spiking neuron that factorizes temporal computation within each neuron into Frequency Selectivity (FS) and Temporal Shaping (TS). The FS module parameterizes each neuron's target frequency as the maximizer of its subthreshold magnitude response, while the TS module reshapes when frequency components contribute to membrane voltage accumulation through group-delay modulation. On auditory benchmarks where frequency selectivity and timing are central to the input structure, FiTS consistently improves over a plain Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) baseline in simple feedforward SNNs without recurrence or network-level delays, while remaining competitive with strong temporal SNN baselines. Beyond accuracy, the learned target frequencies and group-delay shifts provide interpretable neuron-level summaries of the frequency and timing organization learned within the network. Our code is available at https://github.com/kaistmm/FiTS.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). Code is released at https://github.com/kaistmm/FiTS
♻ ☆ Knowledge-Guided Memetic Algorithm for Capacitated Arc Routing Problems with Time-Dependent Service Costs
Qingya Li, Shengcai Liu, Wenjie Chen, Juan Zou, Ke Tang, Xin Yao
The capacitated arc routing problem with time-dependent service costs (CARPTDSC) is a challenging combinatorial optimization problem that arises from real-world applications. CARPTDSC has two main challenges in reducing computational time. First, it is an NP-hard problem. Second, the time-dependent service costs of tasks require frequent evaluations during the search process, significantly increasing the computational burden. These challenges make it difficult for existing algorithms to perform efficient searches, often resulting in limited efficiency. To address these issues, this paper proposes a knowledge-guided memetic algorithm with golden section search and negatively correlated search (KGMA-GN), where two knowledge-guided strategies are introduced to improve efficiency. First, a knowledge-guided initialization strategy (KGIS) is proposed to generate high-quality initial solutions to speed up convergence. Second, a knowledge-guided small-step-size local search strategy (KGSLSS) is proposed to filter out invalid moves, thereby reducing unnecessary evaluations. Experimental results on five benchmark test sets, including both small- and larger-scale instances, demonstrate that KGMA-GN achieves higher search efficiency than the state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the ablation study further confirms that the knowledge-guided local search operators in KGSLSS can significantly reduce runtime compared to traditional operators, especially for the knowledge-guided swap operator, which achieves more than a tenfold improvement in speed.

☆ Evolved Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Seizure Detection: Calcium Dynamics and Delay Mechanics
Tuba Aksoy
Neuroevolution can discover compact network designs that are hard to specify by hand. The EONS framework evolves the topology, weights, thresholds and delays of neuromorphic spiking networks without gradients. We tested whether giving integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons an activity-dependent calcium current (Ca-IF neurons) improves evolved networks for EEG seizure detection, with calcium parameters fixed, shared across a network, or evolved for each neuron. On 10 held-out CHB-MIT patients never seen in training, per-neuron calcium raised the record-level Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.592 to 0.726 over 20 independent runs (p = 0.008) and lowered the false-alarm rate from 0.17 to 0.10. Fixed or per-network calcium gave no significant benefit. IF networks with evolved synaptic delays of 1-3 ticks gave a similar gain (p = 0.005), whereas axonal delays did not. On Siena, with unchanged settings, per-neuron calcium gained +0.096 MCC over IF in one patient-disjoint split (p = 0.011) and +0.059 in the other (p = 0.052). These results suggest that calcium and delays may make the evolutionary search more effective, and motivate testing on more data and in neuromorphic hardware.

♻ ☆ Pulling Back the Curtain on Deep Networks
Maciej Satkiewicz, Roberto Corizzo, Marcin Pietroń
In linear models, visualizing a weight vector naturally reveals the model's preferred input direction, but extending this intuition to deep networks via gradients or GradientAscent often yields brittle or adversarial-looking features. We argue that deep networks are better understood as input-conditioned affine operators, whose natural adjoint action pulls a neuron's preferred direction back to input space. We further refine this representation through optional backward-only softening for hard-gated layers and propose pullbacks as an alternative backward operator for existing explanation procedures, including local attribution, smoothing, and iterative ascent. Across convolutional architectures (ResNet50, VGG) and transformer-based models (PVT), replacing gradients with pullbacks yields improvements in 46 out of 60 comparisons across five faithfulness, stability, and localisation metrics. In particular, PullbackAscent improves mean scores over GradientAscent across all five primary metrics on each architecture, reducing mean Infidelity by factors of 2.8 to 5.5. Strikingly, it also produces sharp, perceptually aligned and target-specific perturbations in only a few steps, without post-processing or explicit perceptual priors. More broadly, pullback-based methods achieve the best mean in 13 out of 15 architecture-metric combinations, outperforming established attribution baselines. Our results suggest that adjoint transport can serve as a reusable backward primitive, enhancing existing explanation procedures without architectural changes or elaborate attribution pipelines. We use "Semantic Pullbacks" (SP) to denote the resulting family of pullback-based explanations.

♻ ☆ RIPE-MambaSpike: Resolution-Independent Spiking-State-Space Interfaces for Parameter-Efficient Event-Based Vision
Md Muhiminul Islam, Shoaib Ahmed Dipu, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury
Spiking-Mamba hybrids reach strong accuracy on event-based vision, but existing designs often require tens of millions of parameters. Much of that cost comes from how the spiking front-end is connected to the state-space backbone rather than from the hybrid architecture itself. In a representative model, a single resolution-dependent projection accounts for 33.55M of 36.25M parameters. To that end, we introduce RIPE-MambaSpike (Resolution-Independent, Parameter-Efficient), which replaces that projection with a hierarchical multi-resolution bridge of fixed channel width. Its deployed footprint is 0.870M parameters, constant at fixed time steps and widths across a 43x range of input areas. Reparameterized spiking stages, temporal decoupled modulation, and a dynamic convex-hull-bounded dual-stream membrane-potential attention preserve accuracy under this compact design. Result-wise, RIPE-MambaSpike is pareto-optimal on CIFAR10-DVS, N-Caltech101, and DailyDVS-200. Notably, on the 200-class DailyDVS-200, a scaled 8.04M configuration achieves 45.7% top-1 accuracy, the best reported spiking result on that benchmark, and outperforms prior spiking methods with 3.0-15.1x fewer parameters than dense ANNs. Overall, our findings demonstrate that competitive event-based recognition does not require resolution-dependent parameter growth. Code is available at https://github.com/MuhiminOsim/RIPE-MambaSpike.

♻ ☆ Empirical Ciphertext Distinguishability Testing of KEMs and Hybrid Encryption via Deep Learning
Simon Calderon, Niklas Johansson, Onur Günlü
We model indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack (IND-CPA) games as binary classification tasks for deep neural networks (DNNs). We apply this methodology to the public-key encryption (PKE) schemes used to construct PQC key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs) such as ML-KEM and HQC, and to cascaded symmetric algorithms, demonstrating methodological generality. Moreover, we present a novel extension of this approach to empirical distinguishability testing of hybrid KEMs. For IND-CPA-secure schemes and their combinations, no DNN achieves accuracy significantly different from random guessing (measured via Bonferroni-corrected binomial tests), consistent with theoretical security guarantees. For insecure schemes, such as plain RSA, AES-CTR and AES-CBC with IV or counter reuse, or RC4, the DNNs classify the ciphertexts better than random guessing. Thus, this framework is shown to serve as a practical, scheme-agnostic tool for flagging distinguishable ciphertexts in both individual and composed constructions.
♻ ☆ Sketch of a novel approach to a neural model
Gabriele Scheler
We present an account of neuroplasticity with respect to cell-internal processing pathways in relation to membrane and synaptic plasticity. We think traditional synapse-centric, weight-based models of memorization are not sufficient or adequate to capture the complexity of neuroplasticity. In these accounts, the model is a network of neurons connected by adaptive transmission links. The adaptation of the transmission links relies on weight changes according to use of the transmission link (short-term and long-term potentiation/depression). In contrast, we propose a paradigm switch from a synapse-centric model (each synapse learns independently, based on its history of use) to a neuron-centric model (each neuron uses signal selection for intracellular pathways to express plasticity at the membrane). A neural model consists of (a) expression of parameters at the membrane, in particular dendritic synapses or spines, and axonal boutons (b) internal parameters in the sub-membrane zone and the cytoplasm with its protein signaling network and (c) core parameters in the nucleus for genetic and epigenetic information. In a neuron-centric model, each node (=neuron) in the network has its own internal memory. Neural transmission and information storage are separated, not automatically combined by coupling strength. There is filtering and selection of signals for storage. Not every transmission event leaves a trace. This represents an important conceptual advance over synaptic weight models. We present the neuron as a self-programming device, rather than as passively determined by ongoing input. We believe a new approach to neural modeling is necessary, because the experimental evidence is not well captured by traditional synapse-centric models. Ultimately, we are interested in the possibilities of a flexible memory system that processes external signals according to its inherent structure.
